description.narrative: The second phase of Australia's Peacebuilding in Conflict-Affected Mindanao investment ($64.5m in 2023-28) supports a more peaceful and prosperous Philippines and a more stable Southeast Asian region by working to counter terrorism and violent extremism. This investment builds on our previous commitment ($92 million, 2014-2023) to support the ongoing peace process between the Government of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). It focuses on reducing the drivers of conflict, helping more combatants return to civilian life, and supporting long-term stability, security, and development in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

description.narrative: Australian supported mediation resolves Clan Conflict in Sulu – where government institutions have limited capacity to provide security and justice – to support safer communities and ultimately reduce violence. ‍ Tumikang Sama-Sama (TSS) is a non-government organisation that mediates clan conflict in Sulu, Philippines. In January 2024, TSS worked to resolve a local armed conflict that had claimed two lives. Engaging security forces and local leaders, TSS negotiated a ceasefire to prevent additional casualties, understand the nature of the conflict, and facilitate mediation. This led to the signing of a peace covenant in May 2024 to resolve the conflict. The signing was attended by the local mayor, community leaders and the military. ‍ TSS is funded under Australia’s Peacebuilding in Conflict-Affected Mindanao investment which supports a more peaceful and prosperous Philippines, and seeks to prevent terrorism and violent extremism.

Australia’s support to the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue (CHD) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), in the Philippines, has improved inclusion in civil society organisations focused on the peaceful prevention and resolution of conflict at the community level. ‍ CHD supported local community organisation Pakigdait to strengthen inclusion, particularly in conflict management, by establishing the “Bae Mediators” Group in August 2024. This collective of women peace mediators is drawn from a Moro Islamic Liberation Front Camp in Lanao del Norte. It works to resolve community conflicts (such as domestic altercations; sensitive and gender‐based offenses) and prevent them from developing into larger, more violent incidents or rido (clan conflict). In 2025, the Bae Mediators comprise 35 women, including five women from the Moro National Liberation Front (a separate former armed group) who live in the vicinity of the camp. Since its formation, the Bae Mediators have handled six cases of community conflicts and settled/resolved four. The Bae Mediators of Pakigdait were awarded First Place in the Civil Society Organization Peace Award by the United Nations Women Asia Pacific in June 2025. ‍ https://wps.asean.org/stories/announcement-peace-award/ ‍ https://asiapacific.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2025-06/id-20250402997-voices-of-peace_cso_june2025.pdf

DFAT’s partner, Relief International supports the “Way to Peace Project” which aims for greater youth engagement in community decision-making, building a culture of peace, and resolving local conflict. Relief International has trained eight youth representatives from the local government unit’s peacekeeping council. As a result, this important conflict resolution mechanism can play a more effective role at the community level. ‍ The trained youth organised culture of peace-focussed community dialogues in their respective barangays (villages) where they identified the top 10 concerns and opportunities for young people. These items were either marked for barangay-level action, such as solid waste management, or were integrated into Annual Investment Plans (AIP). The Way to Peace Project assisted 20 local government units to review their AIPs in order to include and address the findings from the youth dialogues. One example of the integration of ideas from the youth dialogues into the AIPs is the ‘Youth Innovation Fund’, a small grants initiative for youth organisations. ‍ Relief International also worked with 29 government agencies and 21 local CSOs to institutionalise youth involvement in peacebuilding and governance.

DFAT’s partners Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) work to strengthen inclusion in political dialogue and in the policies and practices of key institutions of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), with a focus on women, children and Non-Moro indigenous groups. ‍ IAG and UNDP supported key Indigenous Peoples’ organisations including the BARMM’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples Affairs (MIPA). This support provided technical assistance and legal advice to MIPA and eventually facilitated formal collaboration with MIPA and the national government agency, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP). ‍ As a result of Australia’s support, a Memorandum of Agreement was signed between MIPA and NCIP to formalise their collaboration. Crucially, this support also led to the drafting and adoption of the Implementing Rules and Regulation of the Bangsamoro Indigenous Peoples Act of 2024 to ‘protect, promote, recognise and respect Indigenous Peoples’ rights in the BARMM.

Jenny Escudero, a person with a disability, faced social exclusion and discrimination before discovering economic empowerment through sewing. She initially received hands-on support and skills training through Australia's Accelerate Bangsamoro program (AB). Jenny became an AB program participant through AB’s partnership with the Isabela City Government, Basilan Province and Hapisabela Women Dressmakers Association (Hapisabela). The AB program allowed Jenny to build her business with mentoring and coaching support; product development; and better access to markets. Together with Hapisabela, Jenny built a successful dressmaking business that enabled her to support her family and overcome many challenges. ‍ Jenny credits AB for expanding her horizons and boosting her confidence. In February 2025, Jenny represented Hapisabela at a Women's Economic Empowerment Learning Exchange in Davao City. Her association produced the conference kits thanks to the support of AB. Their products also sold at local and regional trade fairs. Jenny said, “Even if I was born with a disability, I was able to do it. Disability is not a barrier to success." ‍ Jenny’s personal monthly income has increased from an average of AUD16 (during the pandemic) to AUD140 following AB’s support.

Ms. Rawasiya Isirani from the Municipality of Talipao in Sulu, Philippines has a cleft lip. She has difficulty communicating and has experienced extreme bullying. ‍ Rawasiya was skilled in making bubuk (toasted dried fish flavoured coconut), a traditional Filipino cooking ingredient, but struggled to reach consumers and produce large quantities. ‍ With support from the project Accelerate Bangsamoro, Rawasiya began to widen her marketing efforts, showcasing the delicacy to a wider audience. Her bubuk has become a sought-after ingredient, and she can now produce and fulfill customer demand. Through the facilitation of Accelerate Bangsamoro, Rawasiya received sponsorship from USSC (Western Union) for product enhancement and marketing. ‍ During 2023-24, 289 women received support from the project to enhance their economic opportunities.

Pidela Jumaani Absari, the wife of a former Abu Sayyaf militant who recently surrendered to the government, carried the stigma of association with the armed group. It was a label that isolated Pidela from her community in Indanan, Sulu Province. ‍ For Pidela, the Accelerate Bangsamoro (AB) program was transformative. The program offered practical support including product enhancement and design, quality control, and organisational development. The women participants were able to develop new skills and self-confidence. Psycho-social healing helped them process trauma and build solidarity. AB also enabled program participants such as Pidela to create spaces of trust, healing and empowerment. ‍ Pidela now produces and sells high-quality handwoven textiles which enable her to buy supplies and pay school fees for her children. She also purchased her own weaving equipment. Pidela is now earning AUD250 per month, up from AUD80. “I am confident that through weaving, I will be able to provide for my family and help my husband, while still taking care of my children’s needs as they attend school”. Her journey is a powerful reminder of what is possible when women are given safe spaces to heal, tools to grow, and support to lead.

Under the Peacebuilding in Conflict Affected Mindanao program in the Philippines, Australia supported The Asia Foundation (TAF) to provide technical expertise on inclusive policy development to the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliament, relating to two priority pieces of legislation. ‍ As part of this support, TAF facilitated two Southeast Asia regional learning exchanges. The first, conducted in partnership with the Ministry of Social Services and Development and the Office of the Attorney General, was held in Malaysia to inform the proposed Magna Carta for Disabled Persons. The second, with the Bangsamoro Women Commission, brought officials to both Malaysia and Singapore to gain insights on how to improve the current draft of the Gender and Development (GAD) Code. ‍ These learning exchanges enabled discussions on the role of moral governance in public institutions, the integration of inclusive values in multicultural societies, the regulation of Islamic charitable practices, and policies on early marriage. Lessons learnt from these exchanges were shared with the Bangsamoro Parliament, particularly the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and People with Disability (PWDs), further enhancing provisions included in the proposed Magna Carta for Disabled Persons and the GAD Code.
